analysis.one_liner: Taxes large owners $10,000 for every single-family home they hold beyond 75, funding down-payment help.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in either of the two committees it was sent to, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge a $10,000 tax each year for every single-family home an owner holds above 75 homes, with the money going into a new Housing Trust Fund. The fund would pay for grants to state housing agencies for down-payment assistance to homebuyers, with priority given to families buying homes sold off by these large owners. Certain owners are left out, including nonprofits, homebuilders, banks holding foreclosed homes, and owners of federally subsidized housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Families trying to buy their first or next home, who would receive down-payment assistance funded by the tax. The bill is also aimed at the housing market broadly: by making it costly for a single owner to hold more than 75 single-family homes, it pressures large owners to sell, putting more houses in reach of ordinary buyers. Note that its definition of ownership is narrow (a direct majority stake), so it reaches only a subset of large owners.

how_it_helps.text: Owners who hold more than 75 single-family residences would owe $10,000 per year for each home above 75, giving them a strong incentive to sell excess homes.
Revenue from the tax would go into a new Housing Trust Fund for grants to state housing finance agencies for down-payment assistance to families buying homes.
State agencies receiving grants would give priority to families buying homes that a large taxed owner sells, directly connecting the tax to homes coming back on the market.
Related-entity ownership is aggregated, so an owner cannot dodge the tax simply by spreading homes across companies under common control.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and companies with large portfolios of single-family homes (more than 75), including institutional landlords and absentee investors, who would either pay the tax or sell homes. Buyers of those homes, and the tax's own rules impose a $50,000 penalty on anyone who fails to report required purchase information.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large landlords and investor home portfolios

drawbacks.text: The definition of ownership only counts a direct majority interest, so investors holding large stakes below a majority, or through structures the rules don't capture, could avoid the tax entirely.

Several large owner categories are fully exempt — nonprofits, builders and rehabilitators, banks holding homes through foreclosure, and owners of federally subsidized housing — which narrows the bill's reach.

The tax applies only above 75 homes, so owners with dozens of homes but fewer than 76 face no charge at all, and the $10,000-per-home charge is small relative to the value of a home, which may make paying the tax an easy choice for the largest owners.
The trust fund spends only as appropriations Acts allow, so revenue collection does not guarantee the down-payment grants actually flow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims squarely at a real problem — large investors accumulating single-family homes that would otherwise be owner-occupied — and recycles the money into down-payment help. But it is narrow: a 75-home floor and a majority-ownership definition leave many large owners untouched, several favored categories are exempt, and the per-home tax is modest for the biggest players. Even if enacted, its effect on the housing market would likely be limited to the very largest portfolio holders. The bigger obstacle is that it never received any committee action, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither ever took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Jackson of North Carolina introduced the bill on December 6, 2023, joined by Rep. Alma Adams.
The same day, the House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Financial Services Committee, the two committees with jurisdiction over its tax and housing provisions.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed in either committee, and the bill's only listed cosponsor was one member, leaving it without momentum.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so all pending legislation, including this bill, expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large owners of single-family rental portfolios, who face no new tax or sell-off pressure, and the committees' leadership, which never had to take a position.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or recorded floor opposition, so no party split is visible; the bill had only Democratic support (one sponsor and one cosponsor) and no recorded Republican action either way.

industries.industry: Institutional and large individual landlords of single-family homes
industries.note: Owners of more than 75 single-family residences would owe $10,000 per excess home each year, pushing them to shrink their portfolios. The bill's premise is that large investor holdings crowd out ordinary homebuyers.
Firms primarily engaged in building or rehabilitating single-family homes are exempt from the tax, leaving their business model untouched while competitors holding finished homes are taxed.
Owners of foreclosed homes are exempt from the tax, so banks that repossess single-family homes face no charge and face no pressure from this bill to release them to the market.
Tax-exempt 501(c)(3) organizations are excluded from the tax, so affordable-housing nonprofits are not charged for their holdings.
